title: Test The Store

jokes.text: Dwight's talking-head intro: 'I, Dwight Truth I'm in charge of the entire operation' — clearly a grandiose self-introduction undercut by the absurd mangled title
jokes.setup: Dwight sets himself up as the heroic leader of the Sabre store launch
jokes.punchline: The garbled self-important declaration ('Dwight Truth') signals his delusion and incompetence even while boasting
jokes.explanation: Works as a character-comedy beat — Dwight's grandiosity is always funny, and the mangled phrasing underscores his pomposity. Not exceptional, but solidly Dwight.

jokes.text: Erin admits she's afraid of falling off the chair while Dwight insists 'your tiny fingers make the best knots'
jokes.setup: Erin is apparently being used for some physical task — we infer she's helping hang/tie something elevated and is scared
jokes.punchline: 'Your tiny fingers make the best knots' — Dwight's total indifference to her fear, reduced to a functional tool
jokes.explanation: Dwight's utilitarian dismissal of Erin's safety concern is funny and character-true. 'Tiny fingers make the best knots' is a specific, weird detail that elevates it above a generic boss-ignores-employee beat.

jokes.text: Erin breaks from her 'hipster Tabitha' cover identity to whisper to the camera: 'Psst. It's me, Erin.'
jokes.setup: Erin is undercover as a hipster named 'Tabitha' to manufacture hype
jokes.punchline: She blows her own cover by whispering directly to the documentary camera, completely unnecessary since we can already see it's her
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully economical joke. Erin's earnest obliviousness — thinking she needs to identify herself to the camera crew — is perfect character comedy. The 'Psst' before it makes it land even harder. High character integration: only Erin would do this.

jokes.text: Nellie claims she was born in Basildon and 'until the age of 32, I talked like this' then does a thick working-class accent: 'which was bloody horrendous, innit?'
jokes.setup: Nellie presents herself as a self-made woman who transcended her humble origins — a classic motivational speech setup
jokes.punchline: The accent she reverts to is comically exaggerated, and she's completely unselfaware about how ridiculous the whole speech is
jokes.explanation: Nellie's performative class-transcendence speech is funny because she's delivering it with total sincerity to people who don't need inspiring. The accent bit is a good physical comedy beat inferred from the text.

jokes.text: Nellie's escalating list of what's 'lower than dirt': 'Loam, magma, mantle, outer core, inner core'
jokes.setup: Nellie says she 'came from dirt — no, lower than dirt' and asks rhetorically 'What's lower than dirt?'
jokes.punchline: Someone helpfully lists geological layers in ascending absurdity; Nellie picks 'loam' and continues her speech: 'Bloody loam, I came from.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The setup is a cliché ('I came from nothing') and the punchline subverts it with hyper-specific geological taxonomy, then Nellie incorporates 'loam' into her inspirational rhetoric without missing a beat. 'Bloody loam, I came from' is a genuinely quotable line. High economy — the whole sequence is tight.

jokes.text: Nellie: 'I hit rock bottom. When I auditioned for the Spice Girls, I didn't even get a callback.'
jokes.setup: Nellie is building to a serious 'rock bottom' moment in her inspirational speech
jokes.punchline: Her 'rock bottom' is failing a Spice Girls audition — absurdly trivial and self-aggrandizing at the same time
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection — 'rock bottom' primes us for something tragic, and 'Spice Girls audition' deflates it perfectly. Also characterizes Nellie as delusionally self-important.

jokes.text: Someone asks 'Which Spice Girl?' and Nellie answers 'The black one. I never stood a chance.'
jokes.setup: Nellie says she failed a Spice Girls audition
jokes.punchline: She auditioned for Scary Spice — a role for which she is visibly, obviously unqualified by race — and her only commentary is resigned acceptance
jokes.explanation: The economy here is exceptional — four words ('I never stood a chance') do enormous comedic work. The joke depends on Nellie's absolute deadpan and total lack of self-pity. It's the perfect tag to the Spice Girls setup. High quotability.

jokes.text: Dwight's dossier on bloggers: 'Bloggers are gross, bloggers are obese. Bloggers have halitosis. You're gonna love 'em.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is briefing the team on the press/blogger outreach strategy
jokes.punchline: His 'dossier' is just a string of insults followed by an instruction to schmooze them — the contradiction is the joke
jokes.explanation: Dwight's contempt for the bloggers he simultaneously needs is a solid character beat. The pivot to 'You're gonna love 'em' is a good deadpan button. Efficient joke.

jokes.text: Ryan: 'When people see this presentation, they're gonna [bleep] in their pants.'
jokes.setup: Dwight asks if Ryan is ready to give a world-fair-worthy presentation
jokes.punchline: Ryan's response is aggressively profane and weirdly specific — 'bleep in their pants' — the overconfidence masking obvious fragility
jokes.explanation: Competent Ryan-as-delusional-hotshot character beat. The bleep and the specific image is mildly funny, but it's setup for a longer arc. Works as a character-establishing joke.

jokes.text: Dwight assigns Packer as 'the sexual predator who has come to prey on the trendy teenage girls obsessed with the pyramid'
jokes.setup: Dwight is assigning roles: Ryan is the pitchman, Cathy is the 'hot girl'
jokes.punchline: Packer's official job title for the day is 'sexual predator' — spoken aloud in a work briefing with complete seriousness
jokes.explanation: Works because Packer is exactly the character this fits — it's perfect casting, as Dwight says. Dwight's earnestness makes it land; he genuinely thinks this is a legitimate marketing strategy.

jokes.text: Packer's talking-head: 'Schrute's out to get me. But I'm playing the long game. As soon as he messes up, I swoop in like a sexual predator.'
jokes.setup: Packer was just assigned the role of 'sexual predator' by Dwight
jokes.punchline: Packer uses 'sexual predator' as a metaphor for his own ambitions without noticing (or caring) that the metaphor is deeply unflattering
jokes.explanation: Good callback that deepens the joke. Packer has so completely internalized the role that he adopts the language in his own strategic thinking. The lack of self-awareness is the joke — classic Packer character comedy.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'I want to create a sense of wonder and enthusiasm as if, at the end of ET, candy poured out of the screen.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is expressing his vision for the Sabre store experience
jokes.punchline: His analogy is weirdly specific and makes no sense — ET doesn't involve candy, and 'poured out of the screen' is a bizarre image that conflates multiple things
jokes.explanation: A nice absurdist Dwight moment — the ET/candy image is specific enough to be funny and weird enough to be surprising. Dwight's bizarre cultural reference bank is part of his character.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'Speaking of pimples, let's release the bloggers!'
jokes.setup: Dwight just said 'I wanna get goose pimples'
jokes.punchline: He uses 'pimples' as a transition to a joke about bloggers, conflating goosebumps with acne as a cheap shot at bloggers
jokes.explanation: A decent wordplay transition joke. The 'release the bloggers' phrasing (as if they're animals) combined with the pimples callback is efficiently nasty. Not brilliant, but lands.

jokes.text: Andy dismisses Jim mid-sentence: 'Don't care. Tell me later.' then immediately pivots to 'Listen, it's important. You've gotta hear this.'
jokes.setup: Jim tries to tell Andy something; Andy cuts him off
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately makes his own announcement and demands everyone listen — oblivious to the irony of dismissing Jim then demanding attention
jokes.explanation: Solid Andy character beat — his self-centeredness is funny and the irony is immediate and clean. Works as a setup for the black eye reveal.

jokes.text: Meredith overhears 'black eye' as 'black guy in the office': 'Hey, I was on the can. What's this about a black guy in the office?'
jokes.setup: Phyllis asks Andy 'Do you have a black eye?'
jokes.punchline: Meredith, arriving late and mishearing, turns it into a racial misunderstanding — compounded by the casually inappropriate framing
jokes.explanation: A classic mishearing gag. Meredith's obliviousness and the casual crudeness ('I was on the can') are on-brand. The wordplay is functional — not sophisticated, but executed cleanly.

jokes.text: Oscar: 'Since the interesting thing happened till now, so much time has passed, it's like my life is buffering.'
jokes.setup: The office is slowly getting the story of Andy's black eye, with everyone talking over each other
jokes.punchline: Oscar's tech metaphor for impatience — 'my life is buffering' — is precise, witty, and perfectly captures the frustration
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's stronger lines. 'My life is buffering' is an inspired turn of phrase — the tech metaphor fits Oscar's character (analytical, slightly superior) and the joke is supremely economical. High quotability. It's a line people actually repeat.

jokes.text: Andy's 'gang' story: motorcycles, weapons, 'punches were going, and I ducked a few, landed a couple'
jokes.setup: Andy has a black eye and is building to an explanation
jokes.punchline: The story is clearly embellished — vague heroic language ('senseless crime'), Pam's overly helpful 'That's true' and 'Weapons'
jokes.explanation: Andy's embellishment is a slow burn — we know the truth will come out. Pam's minimal corroboration is funny. The joke works as a setup for the payoff revelation later. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Erin's hipster persona mispronounces 'Zooey Deschanel' as 'Zoo-ey Desh-channel' and 'Coachella' as 'Couch-arilla Music Festival'
jokes.setup: Erin is playing an enthusiastic hipster named Tabitha
jokes.punchline: Her hipster cred is undermined by hilariously mangled celebrity and event names — she clearly has no idea what she's talking about
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke. 'Couch-arilla Music Festival' is inspired — it's the kind of mistake only someone who has heard the word but never seen it written would make. Perfect Erin: she's trying so hard and failing so specifically. High character integration.

jokes.text: Andy desperately escalates against calling the police, citing 'neighborhood pride' and shouting his zip code: '1-8-5-0-5... Dash 7-4-2-7!'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to stop anyone from calling the police about the gang that supposedly attacked him
jokes.punchline: His increasingly absurd arguments culminate in frantically yelling his zip code as evidence of civic pride — the desperation betrays that his story is false
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'we settled this on the street' to shouting his zip code is a good comedic arc. His mounting panic transparently reveals the lie. The 'zip plus 4' detail is a nice specific touch.

jokes.text: Toby's reaction when asked to teach self-defense: 'Me?' — then a beat — 'I can't believe you remembered I do self-defense. Um, I'll go put on my cup.'
jokes.setup: Andy suggests Toby teach self-defense to the office
jokes.punchline: Toby's pathetic excitement — 'I can't believe you remembered' — followed by the practical 'I'll go put on my cup' reveals how rarely he's asked for anything and how prepared he is for even this
jokes.explanation: A quietly devastating Toby joke. His genuine disbelief that someone remembered something about him is heartbreaking-funny, then 'I'll go put on my cup' is an unexpected practical detail that gets a second laugh. High character integration — this only works as Toby.

jokes.text: The office collectively cheering 'Yes! Okay!' when Toby agrees to teach self-defense
jokes.setup: Toby is the most pathetic, least respected person in the office
jokes.punchline: Everyone is inexplicably enthusiastic about him teaching self-defense — the enthusiasm is disproportionate and therefore funny
jokes.explanation: A mild ensemble beat. Funny in context but not a joke with much craft — it's situational.

jokes.text: Blogger spots Andy's untouched Sabre phone: 'He's got his Sabre phone on, and he's not even using it. This is a perfect photo for my Daily Fail blog.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has been stressing about getting good press for the Sabre store launch
jokes.punchline: The first blogger photo op is documenting a product fail by one of Dwight's own employees — ironic and immediate
jokes.explanation: Good irony — the press event immediately goes wrong in exactly the feared way. Functional plot-comedy. The 'Daily Fail' name is a nice touch (riff on Daily Mail).

jokes.text: Dwight frantically demonstrates how Jim should have used the phone: 'Hello. Hi, sweetie. It's Jim. I'm calling you from the new Arrowhead...' doing a Jim impression
jokes.setup: Dwight is furious that Jim didn't pretend to use the Sabre phone for a blogger photo
jokes.punchline: Dwight doing a bad impression of Jim — using a patronizing voice and scripted 'ergonomic' product lines — while Jim watches
jokes.explanation: Dwight impersonating Jim is good character comedy — his contempt leaking through the script he's trying to deliver is funny. The elaborate fake phone call he demonstrates is absurd enough to land.

jokes.text: Jim offers: 'Maybe pretend to be Chuck?' and Dwight responds 'You could have pretended to be Chuck. I BEGGED you to pretend to be Chuck — but you chose to be yourself, and you can no longer be Chuck! Surrender the tripack.'
jokes.setup: Jim tries to make amends for the blogger photo incident
jokes.punchline: Dwight's escalating fury — specifically 'you chose to be yourself' as if it's the worst possible decision — and the formal command 'Surrender the tripack'
jokes.explanation: Great Dwight line: 'You chose to be yourself, and you can no longer be Chuck' is wonderfully pompous. 'Surrender the tripack' has the mock-military Dwight formality that makes his character so funny. Good escalation structure.

jokes.text: Dwight trying to operate a camera/projector and failing: 'Point it towards the store, idiot!' and 'One of these buttons is— Damn it. Take over.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is trying to set up a grand presentation element
jokes.punchline: He can't operate the equipment and immediately gives up, snapping at himself and others
jokes.explanation: Generic tech-failure slapstick. The 'idiot' directed at himself is mildly funny, but this is a weak physical comedy beat. Doesn't add much.

jokes.text: Dwight spots elderly visitors: 'The elderly suck the life out of the young. Get them out of here!' then instructs Erin to shoo them away by telling them the pigeon fountain is 'out behind the bank'
jokes.setup: Elderly people have wandered into the Sabre store, apparently thinking it's something else
jokes.punchline: Dwight's unapologetic ageism expressed as a business principle ('suck the life out of the young'), combined with the specific redirect to a pigeon fountain
jokes.explanation: Dwight's casual ageism as operational strategy is on-brand and specific. 'Pigeon fountain' is a nicely precise absurd detail — Dwight clearly knows the neighborhood and has a plan for this scenario.

jokes.text: Toby's self-defense class: 'Strike, scream, and run.' Demonstrates — immediately injures someone. 'Ow.' 'That may have been my fault.'
jokes.setup: Toby is teaching self-defense with apparent confidence
jokes.punchline: The very first demonstration immediately goes wrong and injures a participant; Toby's understated 'That may have been my fault' is the perfect button
jokes.explanation: Classic Toby failure beat. 'That may have been my fault' — delivered in his characteristic flat affect — is perfectly calibrated. The brevity of the disaster (four words of instruction then immediate injury) is structurally excellent.

jokes.text: Toby's 'I-a-a-t-g' acronym: 'It's all about the groin.'
jokes.setup: After injuring someone, Toby tries to recover by teaching a key self-defense principle
jokes.punchline: The elaborate acronym (IAATG) resolves to an extremely simple and crude concept — 'It's all about the groin' — which Toby delivers with total earnestness
jokes.explanation: The acronym build is a good structure — it signals 'important wisdom coming' before deflating to something obvious. Toby's deadpan delivery makes it land. Solid.

jokes.text: Dwight (presumably): hypothetical of a '4'11" man who's penisless' as an attacker scenario — demanding Toby address this specific case
jokes.setup: Toby says 'It's all about the groin' as self-defense advice
jokes.punchline: Someone (almost certainly Dwight given the context and specificity) raises the edge case of a 'penisless' 4'11" male attacker, immediately making it about gender in the most absurd way
jokes.explanation: The over-specification of the hypothetical attacker is absurdist-funny. Toby's follow-up — 'Why are you fixated on this hypothetical transgendered attacker?' — adds another layer.

jokes.text: Toby: 'Why are you fixated on this hypothetical transgendered attacker?'
jokes.setup: Someone has raised increasingly specific edge cases for Toby's self-defense class
jokes.punchline: Toby names the pattern with clinical HR-department precision — 'hypothetical transgendered attacker' — which is both accurate and hilarious as a formal category
jokes.explanation: Toby's matter-of-fact HR framing of the absurd scenario is pitch-perfect. 'Hypothetical transgendered attacker' as a clinical category is very funny. High character integration — Toby's HR-speak is his comedic register.

jokes.text: Andy's self-defense suggestion: 'Show us how to defend ourselves against a baby, and then like a fifth-grade girl, and then, if we have time, on up to a scary man.'
jokes.setup: The self-defense debate has established that Andy got beaten up by a little girl
jokes.punchline: Andy's suggested curriculum starts at 'baby' level and works up to 'scary man' — inadvertently admitting he can't handle a fifth-grade girl
jokes.explanation: A very good Andy joke. The 'baby, fifth-grade girl, scary man' progression is perfectly structured, and Andy delivers it seriously — not realizing he's confessing to needing baby-level training. The specificity of 'fifth-grade girl' (not just 'a girl') makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Andy pivots to a 'point of view of the attacker' question — asking how an attacker can protect himself after getting sucker-punched — and Toby notes: 'It's interesting that you're drawn to the point of view of the attacker.'
jokes.setup: Andy has been maintaining he was a heroic victim; now he's asking for advice from the attacker's perspective
jokes.punchline: Toby's clinical observation catches Andy red-handed; his framing as 'the attacker' reveals the actual incident
jokes.explanation: Great slow-reveal beat. Toby's quiet observation — doing his HR thing — peels back Andy's lie economically. The attacker framing inadvertently breaks Andy's cover story. Well-structured.

jokes.text: Toby mentions 'The latest Chad Flenderman novel, based from the point of view of his nemesis, Dr. Lucifer Wu' as a comparison for perspective-switching
jokes.setup: The conversation about attacker vs. victim perspective
jokes.punchline: Toby has a reference novel called 'Chad Flenderman' (clearly a pulpy thriller) and its villain is named 'Dr. Lucifer Wu' — the name is so over-the-top it's its own joke
jokes.explanation: Toby's pulpy thriller novels are a recurring character detail. 'Dr. Lucifer Wu' is a great villain name — specific, absurd, and somehow very Toby. The non-sequitur nature in a self-defense context is funny.

jokes.text: Meredith: 'Can I please leave? I have a rape flute.'
jokes.setup: Toby is getting sidetracked in his self-defense class
jokes.punchline: Meredith announces she already has personal protection — a 'rape flute' — delivered as a completely mundane factual statement
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Rape flute' is an inspired coinage — it takes the concept of a rape whistle and makes it funnier and stranger. The delivery is everything: Meredith says it as if it's the most normal, practical thing. Extremely quotable. Perfect character integration — Meredith's casual relationship with danger and her slightly chaotic personal life make this completely believable and funnier for it. Economy is near-perfect: five words do enormous work.

jokes.text: Cathy is introduced to 'fatty gruesome, freelancer for Wired Magazine' — actually Patty Grossman, who is a woman
jokes.setup: Dwight introduces Cathy to a blogger she's supposed to flirt with
jokes.punchline: Dwight has completely misidentified the blogger's name and gender; Patty corrects him ('I'm a woman') and Dwight pivots to 'But you still work for Wired, right?'
jokes.explanation: Solid cringe beat. Dwight's total indifference to getting the name and gender wrong — pivoting immediately to 'but you still work for Wired, right?' — is exactly right. His priority is the contact, not the person.

jokes.text: Ryan's pre-presentation meltdown: 'No bleep, Sherlock! Can somebody please tell me something encouraging before I go out there in front of a million people?'
jokes.setup: Ryan is clearly nervous before his presentation
jokes.punchline: His self-aggrandizing estimate of the audience size ('a million people') while having a complete breakdown reveals his ego-fragility simultaneously
jokes.explanation: Ryan's ego-collapse is funny. 'A million people' for a mall tech store opening is a good character-specific exaggeration. Functional.

jokes.text: Dwight's attempt at encouragement: 'You just need to realize so much rides on this. You have no idea.' — then to camera: 'I'm trying to make him feel important.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is trying to calm Ryan down before the presentation
jokes.punchline: His 'encouragement' is actually a pressure-maximizing statement; his explanation to camera ('I'm trying to make him feel important') reveals he has no idea how encouragement works
jokes.explanation: Great Dwight joke. His talking-head explanation — 'I'm trying to make him feel important' — is a perfect example of his total lack of emotional intelligence. The gap between his intent and his execution is the comedy.

jokes.text: Jim improvises a Kelly impression to encourage Ryan: 'Oh, Ryan, you're so smart. You're smarter than Mark Zuckerberg and those Google guys all combined.'
jokes.setup: Jim wishes Kelly were there because 'she always knew what to say' to Ryan
jokes.punchline: Jim does a Kelly impression that's essentially empty flattery ('What's a book?') — but it actually works on Ryan
jokes.explanation: The Kelly impression is a good bit — Jim captures her specific brand of extreme flattery that manages to also be insulting ('You're so ignorant'). The 'What's a book?' exchange is a nice absurdist touch that captures the Ryan-Kelly dynamic.

jokes.text: Jim's Kelly impression continues: 'You're so ignorant, you barely know what you're talking about. That's so ridiculous. You really need to read a couple of books.' Ryan: 'What's a book?'
jokes.setup: Jim is impersonating Kelly's unique brand of backhanded encouragement
jokes.punchline: Ryan plays along — 'What's a book?' — in exactly the vapid way the bit requires, and both of them inhabit this dynamic completely naturally
jokes.explanation: Ryan's 'What's a book?' is a perfect button — he's so into the bit that he commits fully to playing dumb. The Ryan-Kelly dynamic is well-used here. Solid character comedy.

jokes.text: Dwight tries to do the Kelly impression and it fails immediately: 'You can... You can do it, Ryan. And you know that I'm capable of this. You're the only one who can do it, s-sweetie.'
jokes.setup: Jim's Kelly impression was successful; Dwight tries to replicate it
jokes.punchline: Dwight's version is stiff, awkward, and keeps reverting to first-person ('I'm capable of this') — he fundamentally cannot perform warmth
jokes.explanation: Excellent character callback. Dwight's failed impression — especially the confused 'I'm capable of this' line, referring to himself instead of Ryan — perfectly captures his emotional rigidity. The comparison to Jim's fluid version makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Ryan's circular feedback loop: 'I would just fix that one—' / 'Oh, "fix" means you hate it! I knew it!'
jokes.setup: Ryan asks for feedback on his presentation
jokes.punchline: He immediately reframes mild criticism as total rejection and spirals — 'I need something to drink!'
jokes.explanation: 'Fix means you hate it!' is a funny encoding of Ryan's fragility — he's literally programmed to interpret all feedback as rejection. Good character beat.

jokes.text: Ryan's drink order meltdown: 'Not red! Get me something yellow or green from a nearby store. Not red!' — standing there while Jim doesn't move
jokes.setup: Ryan has just spiraled about his presentation feedback
jokes.punchline: He issues an increasingly specific sports drink order, prohibiting red, demanding Jim go to a 'nearby store' — and Jim just stands there
jokes.explanation: Ryan's diva sports drink demand escalates nicely. 'Not red' repeated twice is funny. Jim's implied frozen non-response is a good reaction beat.

jokes.text: Toby, mid-self-defense class: 'Now, if your attacker is willing to defile a corpse, you better stop playing dead right away and just make it known that you're alive.'
jokes.setup: Toby's self-defense class continues with increasingly extreme scenarios
jokes.punchline: Toby matter-of-factly advises against playing dead if your attacker might also be a necrophiliac — delivered with his characteristic HR-manual affect
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The necrophilia escalation is unexpected and perfectly dark. Toby delivers it in the same flat instructional tone as all his other advice — which makes it exponentially funnier. The logic is internally consistent (it IS good advice), making it darkly absurdist. Economy is excellent. Easily quotable.

jokes.text: A woman arrives claiming her daughter had an altercation with 'some fancy gentleman with a squeaky voice' — and points to Andy: 'That's him... The guy I hit.'
jokes.setup: Andy has fabricated a story about fighting a motorcycle gang to cover for his black eye
jokes.punchline: The truth arrives in person: a girl's mother, describing Andy as 'some fancy gentleman with a squeaky voice' — and Andy is identified not as a hero but as the guy the girl hit
jokes.explanation: Excellent payoff to a well-constructed lie arc. 'Some fancy gentleman with a squeaky voice' is a perfect character description that both humiliates Andy and perfectly fits him. The reveal is structured well — the mother arrives, the mystery of who the 'fancy gentleman' is, then the point. This earns an 8 for its structural elegance as a callback/reveal.

jokes.text: Andy's daughter and her father confront Andy at the office — revealing the 'gang' was a 12-year-old girl and her dad
jokes.setup: Andy has spent the episode pretending he was attacked by a dangerous motorcycle gang
jokes.punchline: The 'gang' is revealed to be a little girl (and her father, who describes Andy as 'some fancy gentleman with a squeaky voice')
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the Andy storyline is well-earned — the episode has built this for 8 minutes. 'Fancy gentleman with a squeaky voice' is a great specific detail. High structure score for the sustained misdirection.

jokes.text: Kevin blurts: 'Poor Andy! First you got beat up by a gang, and now she kicks your ass?'
jokes.setup: Andy is being confronted by the little girl who actually hit him
jokes.punchline: Kevin, missing the obvious implication, expresses sympathy for the wrong thing — treating the girl's presence as a new attack rather than the reveal
jokes.explanation: Kevin's obliviousness is on-brand and gets a good laugh. He's processing information a step behind everyone else. Solid character beat.

jokes.text: The mother: 'What about the lady you hit with a pine cone?' / 'There. That chubby one.' — pointing at Pam, who just had a baby
jokes.setup: Andy's lie is fully unraveling; the mother is identifying more victims
jokes.punchline: She describes Pam as 'that chubby one' — Pam's reaction beat follows, then: 'I just had a baby.' / 'Yesterday?'
jokes.explanation: The 'Yesterday?' response to 'I just had a baby' is a great button — the skepticism is mean but the timing is sharp. The cringe of Pam being called chubby is functional Office discomfort comedy.

jokes.text: The girl apologizes: 'Sorry I kicked your ass in front of your "thin" girlfriend.' — with air-quotes on 'thin'
jokes.setup: The little girl is forced to apologize to Andy
jokes.punchline: Her 'apology' includes a passive-aggressive dig at Pam's weight with conspicuous air quotes around 'thin'
jokes.explanation: This is a great subversive joke — the 12-year-old bully's 'apology' is itself a fresh insult, and the air-quotes on 'thin' (directed at Pam who recently had a baby) is brilliantly specific cruelty. The child being crueler than the adult is the comedic inversion.

jokes.text: Girl follows up: 'How 'bout we wait till next year after you have your kid?' — about Pam
jokes.setup: The girl has just insulted Pam with air-quoted 'thin'
jokes.punchline: She doubles down — suggesting Pam's body will be worse after her coming baby — escalating the nastiness while nominally still 'apologizing'
jokes.explanation: A good escalation of the bully-girl joke. The detail that she knows Pam is pregnant and specifically weaponizes it is impressive cruelty from a child, which is the joke.

jokes.text: Girl's dad: 'You know what? Tiffy's going to college.' — said as a final statement of dominance before leaving
jokes.setup: The awkward confrontation has ended with the girl's non-apology
jokes.punchline: Dad closes with the non-sequitur announcement of his daughter's future college prospects — as if this is the ultimate trump card
jokes.explanation: A quietly funny non-sequitur button. 'Tiffy's going to college' as a parting shot — implying his daughter is better than Andy regardless — is an odd, proud-dad thing to say in this context. The economy is good.

jokes.text: Girl's dad: 'Friend of mine uses your paper. You do good work.' — to the Dunder Mifflin employees after everything
jokes.setup: The tense confrontation has just ended; everyone is awkward
jokes.punchline: Dad completely shifts register and gives an unsolicited compliment about their paper business — as if transitioning to networking after a street fight
jokes.explanation: An unexpectedly funny beat. After his daughter has humiliated everyone, dad casually pivots to complimenting their paper business. The total tonal whiplash — from confrontation to networking — is what makes it land.

jokes.text: Toby: 'My ex-wife used to demolish me. No, there is shame in it, okay? We have to draw the line somewhere.'
jokes.setup: Andy says there's 'no shame' in getting beaten up by a girl; the example given is his ex-wife
jokes.punchline: Toby responds 'No, there IS shame in it' — contradicting himself — immediately after revealing his ex-wife 'used to demolish him'
jokes.explanation: Excellent Toby joke. The self-contradiction is perfectly structured — he reveals his ex-wife beat him, then asserts there IS shame in it, drawing the line that he himself has crossed. The resigned self-awareness is heartbreaking and funny. High character integration.

jokes.text: Phyllis: 'Oh my God, I think I see the imprint of a ring pop.'
jokes.setup: Andy has a black eye from being hit by a little girl
jokes.punchline: Phyllis identifies the specific weapon — a Ring Pop candy — from the bruise pattern, which is both funny and humiliating for Andy
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The specificity of 'Ring Pop' as the weapon is inspired — it deepens the humiliation (he was punched by a child who was eating candy at the time) and is completely unexpected. Economy is near-perfect. Highly quotable. The visual implied by the dialogue (Andy's eye showing a Ring Pop imprint) is a great visual gag.

jokes.text: Ryan calls his uncle to get a Ritalin prescription: 'Hey, Uncle Lucas, it's your nephew, Ryan. I could use a prescription for Ritalin right now... I know you did one for Aunt Carol. Oh, so it's different because it's your wife? Well, that doesn't make any sense to me.'
jokes.setup: Ryan is panicking before his presentation and calls his uncle
jokes.punchline: The call reveals Ryan is trying to get an illegal prescription from a family member, citing the precedent of Aunt Carol as his argument — the logic is both absurd and specific
jokes.explanation: Very Ryan. His argument ('you did it for Aunt Carol') is the kind of self-serving, circular logic that perfectly captures his character. The moment is darkly funny because he's trying to get drugs before a work presentation and treating it as a negotiation.

jokes.text: Dwight pitches the remaining bloggers on Ryan: 'We got this young whiz kid — Ryan. He's like an even more handsome Bill Gates.'
jokes.setup: Bloggers are losing interest and drifting away from the Sabre store
jokes.punchline: Dwight's pitch for Ryan is 'even more handsome Bill Gates' — which is a strange compliment given that Bill Gates is not known for his looks, and Ryan is currently having a breakdown
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny. The Bill Gates comparison is an odd choice of compliment that reflects Dwight's limited social toolkit. Functional but not memorable.

jokes.text: Ryan calls his Uncle Lucas from the bathroom asking for a Ritalin prescription, referencing 'Aunt Carol' as precedent
jokes.setup: Ryan is hiding in the bathroom, avoiding his presentation
jokes.punchline: He's calling family members to get prescription medication — the desperation and the specificity (Aunt Carol's prescription) reveals he does this regularly
jokes.explanation: Good character deepening. The Ritalin call is very Ryan — his drug-related past (earlier seasons) is obliquely referenced. The Aunt Carol detail makes it feel like a familiar pattern.

jokes.text: Ryan's text to Dwight: 'I'm sorry. I lied. I'm not in the bathroom. I can't do it. I need to see my mom. I'm going home.'
jokes.setup: Everyone has been waiting for Ryan to emerge from the bathroom for the presentation
jokes.punchline: He reveals he's already left — and the reason is that he 'needs to see his mom'
jokes.explanation: Perfect Ryan collapse. The text message format is efficient; the escalation from 'I'm sorry' through 'I lied' to 'I need to see my mom' is pitch-perfect. 'I need to see my mom' is the funniest part — utterly childish and completely in character for Ryan's regression under pressure.

jokes.text: Old woman at the store tells Erin she's searching for 'handsome men' after being redirected from the Sabre store, and expresses sympathy when told Erin was rejected by Andy: 'Someone rejected you? With that body and those bazongas?'
jokes.setup: An elderly woman has been directed away from the Sabre store and is chatting with Erin
jokes.punchline: She offers surprisingly frank and crude comfort to Erin — 'those bazongas' — a generational mismatch making the language funnier
jokes.explanation: A funny side-scene. The old woman's frank assessment ('bazongas') coming from a grandmotherly figure is the joke — subverted expectations of how elderly women speak. 'Forget your husband' is another good button.

jokes.text: Elderly woman to Erin: 'And you should forget your husband.' Erin: 'Well...' — the implication being that Erin's 'husband' (Andy) is not actually her husband
jokes.setup: The elderly woman has confused Andy for Erin's husband
jokes.punchline: She tells Erin to 'forget her husband' — the irony being that Andy is her ex, not husband, and she can't simply forget him
jokes.explanation: A mild ironic beat. The misunderstanding is gentle and the joke is soft. Works as part of the Erin/elderly woman scene but isn't strong on its own.

jokes.text: Dwight pivots from Ryan's absence: 'As brilliant and creative as he is, he is nothing... compared to this guy!' — pointing at Jim
jokes.setup: Ryan has abandoned the presentation and Dwight has to cover
jokes.punchline: He builds up Ryan before dramatically revealing Jim as the replacement — Jim's reaction is pure horrified confusion
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection structure. Jim's bewildered 'Uh... What?' is funnier than the setup. The pivot from Ryan to Jim is logical in Dwight's world (Jim was Chuck) but absurd in reality.

jokes.text: Jim: 'This is not the face of a performer. This is the face of a scary apparition you see before you die.'
jokes.setup: Dwight needs Jim to give a product presentation to bloggers
jokes.punchline: Jim resists by describing his own face as a death omen — 'a scary apparition you see before you die' — which is both self-deprecating and absurdly dramatic
jokes.explanation: One of Jim's better self-aware lines this episode. 'The face of a scary apparition you see before you die' is a wonderfully dramatic and unexpected image. The escalation from 'not a performer' to 'death omen' is well-structured. Quotable.

jokes.text: Dwight insists there's a costume for the presentation. Jim: 'A costume?' Dwight: 'Of course there's a costume!'
jokes.setup: Jim has reluctantly agreed to give the presentation
jokes.punchline: There's a full costume — which Jim didn't know about — and Dwight treats this as obvious ('of course')
jokes.explanation: Good escalation setup for what's coming. 'Of course there's a costume!' in Dwight's affronted tone is funny — as if everyone should have assumed this.

jokes.text: Dwight hovering outside the changing room: 'Hurry up. Let me in. I wanna watch you get dressed. Did you find the eyeliner?'
jokes.setup: Jim is changing into Ryan's presentation costume
jokes.punchline: Dwight's impatience manifests as an extremely inappropriate request to watch Jim change, immediately followed by asking about eyeliner
jokes.explanation: The Dwight-Jim dynamic is at its best when Dwight's total lack of social awareness crosses into something inappropriate. 'I wanna watch you get dressed' followed immediately by 'Did you find the eyeliner?' is a great one-two.

jokes.text: Jim: 'I'm not wearing eyeliner.' Dwight: 'You are wearing eyeliner, Jim.'
jokes.setup: Jim has just been handed the costume
jokes.punchline: Dwight overrules Jim's objection with complete authority — 'You are wearing eyeliner, Jim' — stated as settled fact
jokes.explanation: Four words: 'You are wearing eyeliner.' The economy is exceptional — Dwight's authority is expressed entirely through declarative certainty. Jim's resistance doesn't matter. A small but very well-crafted moment.

jokes.text: Jim's presentation opening: 'Time. Space. Gender. There are no rules anymore. All boundaries are breaking down in the wake of the infinite future.'
jokes.setup: Jim, in eyeliner and costume, must give Ryan's presentation to the bloggers
jokes.punchline: He launches into maximally pretentious pseudo-philosophical tech-bro speak — clearly reading Ryan's notes with zero conviction
jokes.explanation: The tech-bro pretension of Ryan's presentation script is funny precisely because Jim is delivering it — his natural skepticism must be suppressed. 'Time. Space. Gender.' spoken as revelation is nicely absurdist.

jokes.text: Jim's presentation devolves into personal confession: 'I've been in a relationship that tore my heart apart without ever being able to accept that love drove the pain.'
jokes.setup: Jim is giving a product presentation for the Sabre pyramid
jokes.punchline: He goes completely off-script into personal emotional disclosure about his relationships — as if this is relevant to the product
jokes.explanation: The oversharing-as-sales-pitch is a nice cringe comedy beat. Jim appears to be genuinely working through something — possibly Ryan's notes bled into his own thoughts — which makes the presentation increasingly incoherent and funny.

jokes.text: Jim's presentation continues: 'When I was ten years old, my parents took me to Disney World. I cried the whole time. I was not able to comprehend the beauty that was before me. I just wanted to go home. This is what the pyramid will do for you. It is the bridge to the world.'
jokes.setup: Jim continues reading Ryan's notes, which have become increasingly personal
jokes.punchline: The Disney World childhood trauma is deployed as a product metaphor — the pyramid, like Disney World, is too beautiful for the unready mind — the logical leap is absurd and the connection is completely meaningless
jokes.explanation: Peak absurdism in the episode. Ryan's childhood Disney World crying is deployed as product metaphor, and the pivot — 'This is what the pyramid will do for you. It is the bridge to the world.' — makes no sense but is delivered with complete earnestness. This is exceptional character comedy: it tells us everything about Ryan's self-mythology and the episode uses Jim as an unwilling vessel for it. The 'I cried the whole time' detail is the perfect specific absurdity.

jokes.text: Jim: 'When I was ten years old, my parents took me to Disney World. I cried the whole time. I was not able to comprehend the beauty that was before me. I just wanted to go home. This is what the pyramid will do for you. It is the bridge to the world.'
jokes.setup: Jim is still presenting the Sabre pyramid to bloggers
jokes.punchline: The Disney World story — completely personal, emotionally confused, and ending with crying — is somehow connected to the pyramid's value proposition
jokes.explanation: Genuinely funny absurdist product pitch. Crying at Disney World as a metaphor for the Sabre pyramid is delightfully non-sequitur. The pivot 'This is what the pyramid will do for you' after a story about childhood sobbing is inspired. Earns its laughs through escalating WTF energy.

jokes.text: Jim, landing the product specs with the same gravity as his emotional confessions: 'It has a USB port. Wireless... will be available in 2013.'
jokes.setup: Jim has been delivering the most profoundly incoherent presentation
jokes.punchline: After all the pseudo-philosophy and emotional disclosure, the actual product specs are laughably mundane — USB port — and wireless isn't even available yet
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The deflation after the cosmic pretension is perfectly timed — a USB port and future wireless as the actual payload of all that philosophical buildup. 'Wireless will be available in 2013' is especially funny — delivered deadpan as a feature, when it's actually a damning admission. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: Jim: 'You can play anything from Chuck to Cars 2.'
jokes.setup: Jim is listing the pyramid's entertainment capabilities
jokes.punchline: The range of content is extremely limited — a TV show and one movie — 'Chuck to Cars 2' as if these are the poles of an infinite entertainment universe
jokes.explanation: A sharp product-fail joke. 'Chuck to Cars 2' as the entire content range is brilliantly specific — two quite uncool things presented as a content library. The callback to Chuck (the show within the show) adds a layer.

jokes.text: Jim catches Dwight's eye during the presentation and Dwight gives him a thumbs-up/encouraging signal — the absurdity that this is going well
jokes.setup: Jim has given a chaotic, incoherent, emotionally unhinged presentation
jokes.punchline: Dwight signals that it's going great — either he genuinely thinks so or he's encouraging Jim to continue regardless
jokes.explanation: A visual beat — Dwight's thumbs-up is funny given the train wreck that just happened. Relies heavily on the visual. Moderate impact.

jokes.text: Jim appears to take a bow/finish the presentation — then Dwight hisses 'Psst!' from offstage and Jim realizes he missed something and returns
jokes.setup: Jim finishes what he thinks is the presentation and takes his moment
jokes.punchline: Dwight's offstage 'Psst!' forces Jim back to do something else — the theater of a presentation being corrected mid-bow is a solid physical beat
jokes.explanation: A functional physical comedy beat that sets up the final tagline repeat. Works in context but isn't especially inventive.

jokes.text: After Jim's presentation: Dwight leads the team in celebration. Jim: 'Thank you very much.' Dwight: 'Okay, this isn't over. Let's stay focused, okay?'
jokes.setup: The presentation appears to have somehow succeeded
jokes.punchline: Dwight immediately deflates the moment — 'this isn't over, stay focused' — as if there's no time for the celebration he just started
jokes.explanation: Mild Dwight character beat. His inability to enjoy a moment is funny but it's a thin joke.

jokes.text: Toby's self-defense callback to Andy: 'Little things can be dangerous. Whether it's a Gremlin or Chucky the Doll — the key is to throw it in something. Like a fireplace or a tub of electricity.'
jokes.setup: Toby is continuing his self-defense class with a lesson about small but dangerous attackers
jokes.punchline: 'A tub of electricity' — a completely made-up and impossible defense method, delivered with total confidence alongside the specific horror-movie references
jokes.explanation: A great absurdist Toby moment. 'A tub of electricity' is inspired nonsense — it sounds like something from a horror movie but is physically impossible. Toby's instructional confidence makes it hilarious. 'What is a tub of electricity?' — another character's immediate confusion — is the perfect button.

jokes.text: Reaction: 'What is a tub of electricity?' — another character calls out Toby's nonsense advice
jokes.setup: Toby has just advised throwing small attackers into 'a tub of electricity'
jokes.punchline: The immediate challenge 'What is a tub of electricity?' — flat and literal — perfectly skewers Toby's authority
jokes.explanation: The straight-man callback to Toby's absurd advice. 'What is a tub of electricity?' is a perfect four-word demolition of his credibility. High economy.

jokes.text: Kelly volunteers for the self-defense demonstration: 'I have had a lot of pent-up aggression. Thanks.'
jokes.setup: Someone suggests Kelly attack Toby for the demonstration
jokes.punchline: Kelly's 'Thanks' — as if being told she can attack Toby is a favor being done for her — reveals how much she genuinely wants to
jokes.explanation: Kelly's single word 'Thanks' carrying the weight of genuine gratitude for the opportunity to attack someone is beautifully economical character comedy. Her pent-up aggression is completely believable given her character.

jokes.text: Kelly attacks Toby while yelling: 'You think you're so pretty! Well, you're not gonna be so pretty come prom time!'
jokes.setup: Kelly is supposed to demonstrate self-defense techniques on Toby
jokes.punchline: She launches a real attack while delivering a hyper-specific teenage-girl insult — 'not gonna be so pretty come prom time' — that makes no sense directed at Toby (a grown man)
jokes.explanation: An excellent Kelly joke. 'You're not gonna be so pretty come prom time!' is a brilliantly specific teenage-girl threat delivered against a balding HR manager. The incongruity is perfect — Kelly has instantly reverted to a 16-year-old's psychological warfare. This is the character at her best: petty, escalating, and completely committed. High character integration.

jokes.text: Toby's running commentary during Kelly's attack: 'Okay, this is what's called pre-violent posturing.' Then, after getting hit: 'Okay, I'm at what's called the decision point.'
jokes.setup: Kelly is actively attacking Toby during the demonstration
jokes.punchline: Toby narrates his own assault in HR-manual language as if it's a controlled exercise — 'decision point' — while clearly being hurt
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Toby narrating his own beating in bureaucratic terminology while being actively assaulted is a perfect distillation of his character — passive, procedural, unable to break from protocol even when in danger. 'I'm at what's called the decision point' while being hit is beautifully constructed. High character integration and structure.

jokes.text: Kelly hits Toby in the eye: 'God! My good eye!' — Toby's reaction
jokes.setup: Kelly is attacking Toby in the self-defense demonstration
jokes.punchline: 'My good eye!' implies Toby already has a bad eye — an unexplained detail that deepens his misery
jokes.explanation: Beautifully economical. 'My good eye' is three words that imply a whole history of Toby suffering — there's already a bad eye. It's a perfect Toby joke: his life is so bad that he has a designated 'good' eye. High quotability.

jokes.text: Jim laughs at Toby being hit, then immediately claims he's laughing at 'something Cece did on the playground... yesterday... this morning.'
jokes.setup: Jim is visibly amused by Toby getting hurt
jokes.punchline: He covers immediately with a story about his daughter, but the timeline changes ('yesterday... this morning') under the pressure of lying, revealing the cover story mid-formation
jokes.explanation: Excellent Jim joke. The self-correction from 'yesterday' to 'this morning' in real-time is a beautifully observed piece of lying behavior. The audience can watch the lie being constructed and collapsing simultaneously. Great structure.

jokes.text: Andy's talking-head defense of himself: 'You know why I got hit by girls? Because I stood up for others... Pam and Toby. You may want to ask yourselves, where were you when the girls came?'
jokes.setup: Andy has been humiliated by the revelation that he was beaten by a little girl
jokes.punchline: He reframes his humiliation as heroism — 'where were you when the girls came?' — delivered with total earnestness
jokes.explanation: A great Andy talking-head. 'Where were you when the girls came?' is the perfect absurd martyr statement — completely earnest, totally deluded. The military/heroic rhetoric applied to being punched by a 12-year-old is a wonderful character moment. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Andy's final talking-head: 'Tough day. Yes. But I feel good. I put the office in their place, took a bunch of pain killers, drank half a bottle of wine, took my pants off. I just feel good!'
jokes.setup: Andy is reflecting on his terrible day
jokes.punchline: His coping strategy escalates from 'put the office in their place' (delusional) through painkillers, wine, and removing his pants — all delivered as a list of accomplishments
jokes.explanation: One of Andy's better talking-head moments. The escalation — office, painkillers, wine, pants removal — follows a perfect comedic logic where each item is funnier than the last. 'I just feel good!' at the end, delivered with conviction despite the wreckage, is a great button. High character integration and quotability.

jokes.text: Dwight's final talking head: 'Tough day. Yes. But I feel good. I put the office in their place, took a bunch of pain killers, drank half a bottle of wine, took my pants off. I just feel good!'
jokes.setup: Dwight reflects on the day's events in his confessional
jokes.punchline: Dwight's 'feeling good' is revealed to be chemically and sartorially assisted — pain killers, wine, and no pants — delivered as a non-sequitur series with absolute sincerity
jokes.explanation: A strong ending beat. The escalating list of coping mechanisms — painkillers, wine, no pants — delivered with Dwight's unbreakable positivity is very funny. 'Took my pants off. I just feel good!' is quotable and captures Dwight's deranged pragmatism. The talking head format makes this hit harder.

jokes.text: Nellie delivers the news to Dwight: 'Okay, I will be the first to admit it — we could have integrated more Chuck into the presentation. Dwight. You're the Vice President.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is bracing for bad news about his store launch
jokes.punchline: Nellie leads with a criticism ('more Chuck'), then pivots to giving Dwight the vice presidency — the comedic structure gives the bad news first to subvert expectations
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection structure — the mild criticism before the big win deflates and then inflates in quick succession. The 'more Chuck' caveat is a funny grace note.

jokes.text: Dwight's celebration erupts into wordless physical comedy: 'Ha ha ha ha! Yeah! Okay! Come on! Aah! Right on! Bam, bam, bam, bam, bam! Boom!'
jokes.setup: Dwight has just been told he's the Vice President
jokes.punchline: His victory celebration is completely over-the-top, wordless, and physical — a full outburst of sounds and presumably flailing that continues for nearly 40 seconds
jokes.explanation: Dwight's unhinged victory celebration is funny in performance but relies entirely on Rainn Wilson's physical commitment — there's not much craft in the writing. The extended duration is itself a joke (it keeps going). Impact is higher than craft because the performance does the work.

tmdb_overview: The Florida contingent puts the final touches on the new Sabre store, with Dwight preparing a theatrical presentation in his continuing bid to impress Nellie. Back in Scranton, a red-faced Andy arrives at work with a humiliating injury.
